title: The Signs That Took the Shine
markdown:
The park was a beautiful patchwork of green grass and bright colours, Uncle Theo’s favourite place. His kind hands worked wonders in the soil, helping petunias grow so soft and bright they looked painted by a rainbow. Rosy pinks, deep purples, sunny yellows, each one placed like a precious jewel.

Poppy the squirrel lived in the grand old oak at the park’s edge. Her bushy tail would twitch with a thousand thoughts when she was busy, which was always. She made sure her nest was very neat, polishing each acorn until it shone like a tiny brown star. Not far away, Jun the mole, cheeks as rosy as apples and a nose that wiggled at damp earth, had dug tunnels that his neighbours underground all talked about.

This year the park had a new special addition. Young Timmy, the junior groundskeeper, could make signs. Not just any signs. Wonderfully clear, simply drawn, quite charming. Lines perfectly straight, as if drawn by a ruler made of sunshine, and each one had a friendly little curl at the bottom, like a polite little wave.

Please Mind the Daisies, one sign declared, letters so neat they seemed to hum. Another, near the calm pond: Gentle Ducks Enjoy Quiet Paddles. And tucked among Uncle Theo’s prize petunias: These Blossoms Flourish with Care.

They thanked the signs, not the garden.

Uncle Theo loved quiet moments, the whisper of leaves, the buzz of busy bees, a flower opening to the sun. He spent his days tending, pulling weeds, patiently watering, helping every plant grow its best.

One bright afternoon, a lady wearing a hat the colour of a canary stopped by the petunias. She pointed at the sign. “Oh, how lovely! These blossoms do flourish with care! What a thoughtful sign.”

Uncle Theo, watering can in hand, gave a small happy smile. He had cared, after all.

But then more people started to stop.

“This pond is so peaceful,” a gentleman murmured, looking at Gentle Ducks Enjoy Quiet Paddles. “Whoever put this up really understands peacefulness.”

A little girl, pigtails bouncing, skipped past the daisy patch. “Look, Mummy! Please Mind the Daisies! They’re so pretty, we mustn’t step on them!”

Soon everyone seemed to be praising the signs. Perfect letters. Clear helpful words. The very polite tone.

They thanked the signs, not the garden.

Poppy, from her leafy home, watched. Tail twitching. “Jun,” a worried little squeak, “have you noticed what’s going on?”

Jun popped his head out of a newly dug hole, whiskers quivering. “Noticed what, Poppy? That these carrots I’ve just found are extra crunchy? Because they really are!”

“No, no, not the carrots!” Poppy scampered down. “It’s Uncle Theo! People look at his beautiful flowers, yes, but then they say, What a wonderful sign! They aren’t saying, What wonderful flowers! or What wonderful gardening!”

Jun tilted his head, rosy cheeks puffing. “But the signs are very nice. Quite clear. They tell you exactly what to do.”

“Exactly! But Uncle Theo does all the real work. The signs just… stand there!” A tiny puff of annoyance.

A determined pair, they decided a little investigation was needed.

Meanwhile Uncle Theo, straw hat shading his thoughtful face, was starting to feel like a forgotten bloom in his own garden. He loved his park, but a small word of praise for careful weeding, a compliment on perfectly turned compost, would have been so nice. Many, many hours helping those petunias. And all anyone seemed to notice was the polite little sign nearby.

The next morning Poppy and Jun found a cosy hiding spot behind a big leafy rhododendron and started to watch. A family walked past. The father stopped right in front of Please Mind the Daisies. “Very clear. Such nice writing. Young Timmy is a real artist, don’t you think?”

The mother nodded. “And so polite! I feel I must tread as carefully as a mouse!”

Jun whispered, “They don’t even seem to see the daisies, Poppy. They’re looking at the words!”

Poppy’s tail puffed like a tiny furry explosion. “It’s like they’re thanking the words for being nice, not Uncle Theo for making the flowers nice enough to need minding!”

They kept watching as people admired Gentle Ducks Enjoy Quiet Paddles, while the ducks themselves, plump and happy, waddled by unnoticed. The signs had become the main stars of the park.

They thanked the signs, not the garden.

Then a small sad idea grew in Uncle Theo’s mind. He found a small smooth piece of wood and, dipping a fine twig into berry juice, painted a tiny sign in shaky from-the-heart writing: These Petunias Cherish Your Kind Eyes. He placed it right in the middle of his most beautiful soft petunia.

Poppy and Jun watched, little hearts sinking. A woman with a very big colourful hat stopped. Looked at Uncle Theo’s sign. “Oh, how sweet! This sign is so charming! Your Kind Eyes! What a lovely thought.” She smiled at the sign, then walked away, eyes still fixed on the polite painted words.

Uncle Theo sighed, as soft as autumn leaves. Even more forgotten. The park, usually buzzing, felt a little quieter, a little less bright.

Poppy and Jun scurried over. He was gently trimming a stray leaf from a rose bush, shoulders slumped. “It’s like nobody sees me,” he murmured. “Or my flowers. Just the signs.”

Poppy nudged him with her nose. “But we see you, Uncle Theo. And we see your flowers. They are the very best flowers in the whole wide world.”

Jun nodded hard, nose wiggling. “They smell like sunshine and joy!”

They sat in comfortable quiet, distant birds. Uncle Theo managed a small shaky smile. So good to have friends who truly saw him.

But seeing wasn’t quite enough. Something needed to be done. Poppy, quick and clever, and Jun, strong capable paws, put their heads together. “We need to remind everyone that the signs are just telling us about the wonderful things Uncle Theo has made.”

They helped him. Poppy collected fallen leaves in russet and gold, and tiny colourful petals. Jun created a soft welcoming bed of the richest earth. Together they arranged his most beautiful flowers in a prominent spot near the park entrance.

Then they found a large smooth grey stone. With more berry juice they helped him paint a truly special message. Not a polite instruction like Timmy’s signs. A thank you, painted with love. Thank you for noticing. These flowers bloom because of care.

They placed the stone and the vibrant arrangement where many people would see them.

The next morning, visitors’ eyes were drawn to the bright blooms and the simple heartfelt stone. They paused. They read.

A little boy, instead of rushing toward Please Mind the Daisies, ran directly to Uncle Theo tending his roses. “Mr Theo, your flowers are so pretty! And this stone says thank you for noticing! I do notice!” He pointed to the magnificent petunias. “They’re the best!”

Soon others followed. From the signs to the flowers, from the flowers to the stone, and then to Uncle Theo as he worked, they began to thank him.

“Your roses are simply magnificent!”

“These petunias are truly glorious!”

“Thank you for making our park so beautiful.”

Uncle Theo’s smile spread, bright and warm as midday sun. Straw hat a little straighter. Eyes sparkling.

Poppy, from her oak, felt a deep contented twitch. Jun, peeking from his hole, wiggled his nose with pure happiness. The park had found its happy balance. The signs were still clear and friendly, but now everyone remembered to thank the gardener, too.

They thanked the garden. And the signs, at last, knew how to share.
characters: Poppy (a squirrel), Jun (a mole), Theo (a gardener)
